Saudi authorities apparently [turned
off](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/saudi-warning-system-stayed-
silent-before-deadly-airport-attacks-2026-10-12/) Saudi Arabia's emergency
mobile phone alert system last week - not because Houthi attacks had subsided
- but because, amid complaints that mobile alerts were disrupting residents'
sleep, they hoped to return a sense of normalcy to the kingdom. They did not
succeed. Tennis star Novak Djokovic will [no
longer](https://www.reuters.com/sports/tennis/six-kings-slam-tournament-saudi-
arabia-postponed-december-2026-10-14/) be playing in Saudi Arabia this month;
Saudi Aramco headquarters [was on fire](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-
east/aramcos-dhahran-hq-suffered-extensive-damage-tuesdays-attack-sources-
say-2026-10-14/) Wednesday; and [flights to Riyadh have been
canceled](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/skies-over-saudi-capital-
riyadh-largely-empty-after-deadly-houthi-strikes-2026-10-12/) after a
succession of Houthi missile attacks this week, the most shocking - at least
to the visitors and investors the Saudi government hopes to attract - a strike
Saturday on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 and wounded
hundreds.

These attacks on civilian infrastructure are the latest war crimes in a
conflict replete with criminality and civilian suffering, but also a jarring
demonstration of the destruction that the Houthis are willing and able to
inflict on their neighbor to the north. And Riyadh's decision to turn off air
raid alerts suggests they'll be suing for peace sooner rather than later.
